transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-04-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Sarah Mitchell (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Mike Alvarez (NovaSearch CTO), Priya Nair (PM), Liam O'Connor (ML Eng)

--- Optional auto-summary ---
(automated) Summary: exploring embeddings + reranking, vector DB integration options, throughput targets ~300-1000 RPS, hybrid search, security/compliance questions.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Sarah: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we really appreciate you taking the time. I'm Sarah from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Daniel, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Mike: Good, thanks. Ready to dive in.
[00:11] Priya: Hi, thanks, excited to chat.
[00:14] Daniel: Hi all. Quick agenda — 1) understand your current search pipeline, 2) talk through embeddings + reranking options and vector DBs, 3) performance/throughput expectations and hosting modes (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private), 4) security/compliance and next steps. Sound good?
[00:25] Mike: Yep, sounds good.

[00:28] Mike: To kick off, quick background: NovaSearch is a B2B vertical search product for e-commerce catalogs. We currently run BM25 on Elasticsearch for retrieval, then a small transformer-based reranker in a microservice. At peak we see around 600 RPS across regions, tail latencies matter a lot, and relevance improvements drive revenue. We're evaluating moving to an embeddings-first pipeline to improve semantic recall and to consolidate reranking into a single model flow.
[00:50] Sarah: Great, that's helpful. Do you have an embedding model in mind (open model vs managed) and what dimensionality are you expecting?
[00:59] Liam: We're prototyping with a 768-d model from a community repo — works okay — but we're curious about 1024 or 1536 dims for better quality. Cost is a concern though; higher dims = larger vectors = more storage, slower NN ops.
[01:13] Daniel: Totally. There's that trade-off. For many e-commerce workloads 768-1024 hits a sweet spot, but we often recommend running a small A/B with a 512/768/1536 sample to measure delta. Also think about using quantization (8-bit or 4-bit storage) on the vector DB side — reduces storage and can speed ANN ops.
[01:32] Priya: On the vector DB, we're considering Pinecone because of familiarity, but we've had infra folks look at Milvus and Weaviate. What's Redwood's stance on integrations?
[01:42] Daniel: We integrate with any standard ANN backend — Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate, FAISS on-prem. For Hosted tests we typically prototype using Pinecone or our internal managed index to reduce setup friction. For Dedicated or Private, customers often run Milvus/FAISS inside their VPC or use dedicated producers. There are small differences: Pinecone handles some scaling automatically, Milvus gives you more control.
[02:01] Mike: How does the reranking step fit — do you do retrieve-then-rerank in Redwood or is that something we host?
[02:08] Daniel: Redwood can host the reranker as part of the inference pipeline. Two common patterns: 1) client does ANN retrieval (vector DB) -> returns top N -> calls Redwood for reranking (we run a cross-encoder or instruction-following model) OR 2) Redwood performs both retrieval and rerank if you use our managed index (we'll call the vector DB or maintain an index). Many customers use hybrid BM25 + ANN: recall from BM25 + ANN to ensure lexical matches, then rerank with our model for final ordering.
[02:36] Priya: We're particularly interested in hybrid search because product SKUs and exact name matches still matter. How do you combine BM25 and ANN in practice?
[02:44] Daniel: Usually two approaches: union retrieval — take top K from BM25 and top K from ANN, dedupe, then rerank — or scoring fusion — normalize scores and merge. We often recommend union followed by rerank for best practical results. Important to instrument and compare with your baseline KPIs (CTR, add-to-cart, revenue per session).
[03:06] Liam: For throughput, what's realistic? If we target 600 RPS sustained, with peaks at ~1k, what's the Hosted cost and latency implication?
[03:15] Sarah: Short answer: Hosted is fastest to get started — low ops — but for sustained high RPS and strict tail latency SLOs customers move to Dedicated. Daniel, want to add concrete numbers?
[03:23] Daniel: Sure. For embedding generation we can do batching to improve throughput; on our Hosted we see per-request embed latency ~30-60ms for single calls depending on model and batch size. For rerank cross-encoders, single-shot can be 40-200ms depending on model size. If you need sub-100ms tail, Dedicated with pinned GPUs and optimized kernels is the way to go. For 600 RPS, you'll want autoscaling + batching strategies; Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower unit-cost.
[03:48] Mike: Any guidance on batching vs latency trade-offs? We can't increase UI latency above ~200ms.
[03:54] Daniel: Batching helps cost and throughput but adds queuing latency. A mixed strategy: prefix caching for common queries, small micro-batches (2-8), and dynamic routing where urgent low-latency requests go to a low-latency pool. Redwood's routing policies support that — can route by priority and fall back to cheaper pools.
[04:12] Priya: On data residency and compliance — we need SOC2 and ability to use our KMS for key management if we go Private. What are the options?
[04:21] Sarah: We have Hosted with SOC2 and encryption at rest, plus Dedicated with customer VPC peering and Private deployments where you manage the control plane and KMS/HSM. We'll send the SOC2 summary and KMS integration docs after this call.
[04:34] Mike: Cool. Another thing — vector dimensionality impacts the index layout and cost. Any recommendations on storage and ANN configuration?
[04:42] Daniel: For 768-1536 dims we recommend product-specific configs: smaller dims => HNSW works well with lower memory; larger dims might benefit from IVF+PQ or quantized indexes. Use product filters (metadata) to reduce search scopes. Also monitor recall vs latency and try product-specific thresholds.
[04:59] Liam: We use attribute filters (category, brand) already. If we do hybrid, do we store embeddings in both Elasticsearch and a vector DB? That's duplication.
[05:07] Daniel: Yes, some customers store minimal embeddings in Elasticsearch or store dense vectors as payloads for small catalogs. For large scale, maintain a vector store plus a metadata store. If storage duplication is a concern, consider storing compressed vectors or use index sharding with TTL on older vectors.
[05:22] Priya: Any gotchas when moving from BM25-only to embeddings?
[05:26] Daniel: Beware of cold-start — embeddings can miss exact tokens like SKUs; hybrid helps. Also re-evaluate query pipelines, synonyms, and tokenization. Metrics to track: recall@K, MRR, latency percentiles, and business metrics like conversion.
[05:41] Mike: About the reranker model — do customers typically use a cross-encoder on top-K or a lighter pointwise model?
[05:48] Daniel: Cross-encoders tend to give the best ranking quality but are heavier. A common pattern: dense retrieval with a bi-encoder for fast recall, then a cross-encoder for final N up to 50. Another approach uses a lightweight transformer for quick re-scoring and then a heavyweight cross-encoder for high-value queries. Redwood supports both.
[06:05] [background noise / crosstalk] Liam: Sorry — can you talk about metric collection and the Console?
[06:10] Sarah: Sure — Redwood Console gives per-route token/cost breakdowns, latency histograms, and you can trace individual requests. For rerank we show per-model latency and cost; you can set alerts for quality regressions tied to eval prompt sets.
[06:26] Priya: For a pilot, what would you suggest we run?
[06:29] Daniel: Proposed pilot: 1) ingest 10k sample docs, 2) run embeddings with two dims (768 and 1536) across your query set, 3) compare retrieval recall & rerank quality vs baseline, 4) test with both Pinecone and a local FAISS index to measure latency. We'll provide a benchmark template.
[06:47] Mike: Who owns the vector DB provisioning? We prefer minimal infra for pilot — don't want to spin up clusters.
[06:53] Sarah: For pilot we can manage an index for you on Hosted or set up a small managed Pinecone instance. If you want zero infra, use Hosted managed index to iterate quickly and then switch to Dedicated/Private if you like the results.
[07:05] Liam: We're also evaluating cost — can Redwood provide per-call pricing examples for embeddings + rerank?
[07:11] Sarah: Yes — we'll send example spreadsheets. High-level: embeddings cost per vector generation; search cost depends on vector DB (managed vs self-hosted) and rerank cost per token for the model. Dedicated lowers unit compute cost; we'll include rough totals for your RPS profile.
[07:23] Priya: Any concerns about vendor lock-in if we use Redwood-managed index?
[07:27] Daniel: We build export paths — you can export embeddings and index snapshots. Many customers prototype on Hosted and then run the index in their VPC or in Pinecone. We recommend keeping a reproducible pipeline for embedding generation to avoid drift.
[07:40] Mike: Ok, last piece — SLA and uptime. For Dedicated, what do you offer?
[07:45] Sarah: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and predictable latency targets; plus support SLAs. For Private installs we can do enterprise agreements with longer lead times. We'll surface the details in the contract packet.
[07:58] [00:08 pause]
[08:06] Priya: Quick product question: what about hybrid search ranking heuristics? Can we tune weight between BM25 score and ANN similarity?
[08:12] Daniel: Absolutely — in the fusion step you can tune weights, thresholds, and also use metadata re-weighting. We usually recommend running a grid search on your dev queries to pick weights.
[08:22] Liam: If we go Dedicated, how hard is migration from Hosted?
[08:26] Daniel: We support migrations — configuration and model artifacts are portable. For the index you'd either export or set up replication. We'll produce a migration runbook.
[08:36] Mike: Cool. That addresses most of our technical concerns.
[08:40] Sarah: Great — to recap next steps: Sarah will send security docs and pricing, Daniel will send benchmark plan, Liam will share sample data. We'll schedule a follow-up to review benchmark results and Dedicated pricing — suggested 1 week. Anything else?
[08:55] Mike: No, that's good. Thanks everyone.
[08:58] Priya: Thanks.
[09:00] Daniel: Thanks all.
